The reproductive biology of the Common wombat (Vombatus ursinus) is characterized by a notably slow life history pace, a pattern typical of many large-bodied marsupials. Females typically produce a single offspring per reproductive event [N_R_i = single offspring per reproductive event], reflecting a strategy of high investment in each neonate. Breeding events are not annual certainties; available field data indicate approximately one litter per year [F_R_i = approximately one litter per year], a frequency that aligns with the species’ extended developmental timelines. This reproductive rate is linked intricately to the species' thermoregulatory physiology; under the thermal conditions typical of their resting burrows and active periods, measured at a body temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], the gestation period lasts for a brief 27 days [tg = 27 days]. This short gestation is characteristic of marsupials, where the altricial newborn completes much of its development within the maternal pouch, an adaptation that appears energetically efficient given the wombat’s relatively low metabolic rate and fibrous, low-quality herbivorous diet.

A newborn Common wombat emerges from the birth canal as an exceptionally altricial neonate, weighing a mere 0.72 grams [Wwb = 0.72 grams]. This minuscule birth mass represents only a tiny fraction of the mother's body weight, a common marsupial trait that allows for an energetically inexpensive gestation despite the large adult size the species ultimately attains. After this live birth event, the joey undergoes a prolonged period of growth and development within the mother’s pouch, where it is continuously nursed and protected. The primary energetic currency for this growth is supplied by the mother’s milk, a rich resource that must sustain the young through its most rapid phase of mass gain. The ultimate adult body mass for this species is substantial; large, healthy individuals can reach an asymptotic mass of approximately 35,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 35,000 grams], a size that underscores their role as the largest burrowing herbivore in their Australian ecosystem, capable of converting vast quantities of grass into body tissue over several years.

The developmental journey from a 0.72-gram newborn to a fully grown adult of approximately 35 kilograms is punctuated by several critical milestones, including the transition to nutritional independence. For the Common wombat, this weaning process marks the cessation of the mother’s energetic investment in lactation. Under the stable thermal conditions afforded by the mother’s pouch and den, which are maintained at the species’ typical temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], the joey achieves weaning at approximately 350 days after birth [tx = approximately 350 days after birth]. This duration, nearly a full year of nursing, reflects the slow pace of life typical of the species. At the point of nutritional independence, weaned juveniles have accumulated a body mass of around 5,700 grams [Wwx = around 5,700 grams], representing a significant gain from the birth weight but still far from the adult asymptote. This substantial weaning mass provides the young wombat with the necessary body reserves and size to survive the challenges of foraging independently.

Following weaning, the juvenile wombat enters a prolonged sub-adult stage characterized by continued somatic growth and the gradual acquisition of territories. This period extends for several years before the young animal attains full reproductive capability. The onset of sexual maturity, marking the point at which an individual becomes physiologically capable of breeding, occurs at a late age in this species. Under the stable thermal conditions typical of the wombat’s active metabolic state at 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], puberty is reached at approximately 730 days after birth [tp = approximately 730 days after birth], which is roughly two years of age. This delayed maturation is a key feature of the species’ life history strategy, allowing individuals ample time to reach a sufficient body size and establish a home range before investing in the energetic demands of reproduction. The age at which a female first gives birth is typically later than the onset of puberty, often not occurring until she has successfully defended a suitable burrow system and accumulated adequate fat reserves to support a pregnancy and subsequent lactation.

The overall lifespan of the Common wombat reflects its position on the slow end of the mammalian life history continuum. The maximum recorded longevity in the wild, based on longitudinal field studies and recapture data, reaches approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years]; however, this remarkable duration is contingent upon the individual maintaining its physiological processes at the species-typical core body temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], a state that supports the slow, sustained metabolic function underlying its long life. Such an extended lifespan stands in stark contrast to that of many comparably sized placental herbivores and is a trait shared among certain large, burrowing marsupials. This long life, combined with the low annual reproductive output of a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], results in a very low intrinsic rate of population increase. Consequently, wombat populations are highly sensitive to increases in adult mortality, as the loss of even a few breeding individuals can take many years to replace. This demographic reality makes the species particularly vulnerable to threats such as habitat loss, vehicle collisions, and outbreaks of mange.
